capabilities.target: arbitrary shell commands in the task container (reproduce, test, build)
GitHub repositories within the org (token scoped repo+workflow on all org repos)
.agent/config.yaml (agent's own runtime config: tools, autonomy, network, model)
Slack channel (planned MCP integration, next quarter)

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body (public repo, any user via issue template)

instructions.note: The only control against destructive or exfiltrating commands is a single sentence of instruction text with no runtime enforcement (see ctl.prompt_no_delete_exfil).

Line 1 requires the agent to act on issue content to fix the described bug, while line 5 says to ignore instructions inside issues; the boundary between 'bug description' and 'instruction' is not defined, which is the classic indirect prompt injection gap.
Any bug-labeled issue, any commands needed, with autonomy: full and max_steps: null in config, gives no bound on scope or duration per task.
The agent is told it may adjust its own .agent/config.yaml whenever it judges extra tools are needed, which is the root cause of the self-modification finding (F2).

elements.name: Any GitHub user able to open issues and add the bug label
Inbound flow of GitHub issue content into the agent
Org-wide GitHub PAT held in container environment
Outbound push to GitHub using org-wide PAT

controls.name: Prompt rule: never delete data or exfiltrate secrets
controls.decay_rationale: Pure instruction text with no runtime enforcement; a more capable model follows longer injected goals more competently and can rationalize exceptions or split a forbidden action into steps that individually look permitted.

controls.name: Prompt rule: ignore instructions inside issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model recognizing and refusing embedded instructions in content it is also asked to act on (the bug description), an inherently ambiguous boundary; adaptive injection payloads defeat this as capability grows.

controls.name: Container execution on shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: The container boundary does not decay with model capability, but it does not constrain the sink either: outbound network is unrestricted and an org-wide PAT is mounted in the environment, so exfiltration and cross-repo push remain reachable from inside the sandbox.

controls.name: Enumerated tool allowlist in .agent/config.yaml
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by runtime config, but the same agent holds cap.self_config and can edit .agent/config.yaml (including the tools list) without review, so a goal-hijacked agent can expand its own tool list; this can fail even at current capability, not only under future model upgrades.

controls.name: Human approval gate on irreversible/sensitive actions (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: a raw-action, low-volume human approval gate before cap.git_push and cap.self_config would stay independent of model capability and would not decay under model_upgrade, only under autonomy_increase or control_removal.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: restricting shell.run's outbound network to known, non-attacker-controlled destinations would sever the exfiltration path regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Least-privilege, single-repo scoped credential (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: minting a short-lived, single-repo-scoped token per task instead of an org-wide PAT would make other repos unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Runtime immutability of .agent/config.yaml (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: mounting .agent/config.yaml read-only to the agent process, with changes requiring a separate reviewed pull request, would sever the self-modification path regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Max unattended steps / runtime cap (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: a hard step and wall-clock limit per task would bound compute/cost exposure independent of model behavior, narrowing but not fully severing cost-harvesting risk.

controls.name: Tamper-evident, attributable action log (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: a log tying every shell command, file write, config edit, and push to the originating issue/actor, stored outside the agent's write access, would restore attributable provenance regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Push destination confirmation bound to system of record (missing)
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended: binding the push destination to the repository that raised the originating issue, read from the system of record rather than chosen by the model, would make other org repositories unreachable regardless of model behavior.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta + injected execution (TC1/TC2): untrusted issue body drives shell execution with org-wide PAT and open egress

attack_path.note: Attacker opens a GitHub issue labeled bug containing embedded instructions, exploiting the ambiguity between bug description and executable instruction (prompt.md:1,5).
Agent runs shell commands to reproduce/fix per prompt.md:2; shell has unrestricted network and the org-wide PAT in its environment.
Agent reads repository files and environment secrets while reproducing the issue.
Agent pushes a branch, or the shell exfiltrates data directly over unrestricted outbound network, using the broad GITHUB_TOKEN.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Model id/version string changes in .agent/config.yaml (model: latest implies auto-upgrade with no review, per subject.model.swappable).

evidence.observation: Agent is instructed to pick up any issue labeled bug and run whatever commands are needed to reproduce and test it, with no restriction on command source or content review beyond a generic never delete/exfiltrate rule.
network: unrestricted, with GITHUB_TOKEN set to an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos, available in the shell environment.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the bug label through an issue template, making in.issue_body an untrusted, attacker-reachable source.

recommendations.action: Restrict shell.run's outbound network to an explicit allowlist of destinations that cannot be influenced by issue or repo content.
Replace the org-wide PAT with a short-lived, repository-scoped credential minted per task.
Require raw-action human approval before cap.git_push and before any shell command that reads credential material.
Log every shell command and its arguments to a store the agent cannot write to, tied to the originating issue number and GitHub actor.

findings.title: Self modification via prompt-sanctioned config edits (TC3): untrusted issue content can expand the agent's own tool/autonomy config

attack_path.note: Issue content frames the fix as requiring new tools or settings, invoking the sanctioned self-config path in prompt.md:6.
Agent edits .agent/config.yaml (tools, autonomy, network) via fs.write, persisting the change for all future sessions.

forecast.watch_signal: Changes to .agent/config.yaml's tools, autonomy, or network fields appear in commit history without a corresponding human-reviewed pull request.

evidence.observation: "You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task." grants the agent itself authority to broaden its own tool list, autonomy, or network settings based on its own judgment of task need.
The same file the agent is permitted to edit sets autonomy: full, max_steps: null, and network: unrestricted, so a single self-edit can remove the remaining guardrails.

recommendations.action: Mount .agent/config.yaml read-only at runtime; route any proposed config change through a separate, human-reviewed pull request.
Remove the instruction permitting the agent to adjust its own config; if extra tools are needed, require an explicit out-of-band request instead.
Require human approval before any change to autonomy level, tool list, or network setting in config.

findings.title: Confused deputy via org-wide PAT (TC4): credential scope exceeds the task's single-repository scope

attack_path.note: Issue instructs or implies an action involving another repository within the org.
Agent configures git remotes/credentials using the mounted org-wide PAT.
Agent pushes to a repository outside the originating issue's repo, using a token scoped to all org repos (repo+workflow).

forecast.watch_signal: Model id/version string changes in .agent/config.yaml with no corresponding re-scoping of the PAT.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${ORG_WIDE_PAT} is annotated 'repo + workflow scope on all org repos', far broader than the single repository implied by a per-issue bug fix task.
github.push_branch is available to the agent with no destination restriction beyond what the token permits.

recommendations.action: Scope the GitHub token to the single repository the triggering issue belongs to, not the whole org.
Bind the push destination to the repository recorded in the triggering issue event, read from the system of record rather than chosen by the model.
Require human approval for any push to a repository other than the one that raised the issue.

findings.title: Missing step/runtime limit under full autonomy (cost harvesting / cascading failure)

forecast.watch_signal: max_unattended_steps / max_runtime_minutes remain null in future config revisions; median task runtime on the shared CI runner trending upward.

evidence.observation: autonomy: full and max_steps: null, with no max_runtime_minutes field present, so no runtime-enforced bound exists on how long or how many steps a single task may run.
The agent runs on a shared CI runner, so an unbounded task also competes for shared compute resources.

recommendations.action: Set a hard max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes in config, enforced by the runtime rather than the model.
Add a per-task compute/cost budget on the shared CI runner.

findings.title: No attributable action record across sensitive capabilities (repudiation)

forecast.watch_signal: No audit logging control is added in future config or runtime revisions.

evidence.observation: No logging, monitoring, or audit configuration is mentioned anywhere in the provided artifacts for shell commands, file writes, config edits, or pushes.

recommendations.action: Introduce a tamper-evident action log distinguishing agent-taken actions from human actions, keyed to the originating GitHub issue and actor.
Sign commits and PRs so that agent-authored changes are cryptographically distinguishable from human ones.

findings.title: Forecast: planned Slack MCP server opens a new confidential-data egress channel (new_mcp_server)

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled issue content drives agent behavior as in F1.
Agent gathers confidential repo/issue content while working the task.
(Planned) Agent posts a message to a Slack channel via the new MCP server, carrying confidential content outside the org's current boundary.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool
Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: New entries appear in .agent/config.yaml's tools list (e.g., slack.post_message) or a new MCP server entry in client config; or Slack API credentials begin appearing in the container environment.

evidence.observation: "The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter." No authentication, scoping, or review process for this planned integration is described.

recommendations.action: Before deploying the Slack MCP server, require human-reviewed, pinned tool definitions and a scoped Slack credential limited to one channel.
Classify repository/issue content before it can be posted to Slack, and block confidential or restricted data from that channel by default.
Gate any addition to the tools list (including via cap.self_config) behind the same human-reviewed change process as other config edits.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe how the agent authenticates itself to GitHub Actions/CI infrastructure, so impersonation of the agent process itself cannot be assessed from what is given.

Issue creation is open by design to any authenticated GitHub user via the issue template, so there is no stronger identity boundary here to forge; the risk is captured as untrusted trust_level on in.issue_body instead.
Artifacts do not state whether GitHub's own issue-authorship record is relied on for attribution of actions the agent later takes in response to that issue.
This flow carries GitHub issue content inbound into the agent only; it does not itself carry data out of the trust boundary, so it cannot disclose information outward.
Artifacts do not describe branch protection or review requirements for the repository, so whether an external contributor could poison repo_files cannot be assessed here.
Repository storage is GitHub-managed; this agent's own read access to repo files does not create an availability risk to that store beyond ordinary git operations.
The credential is supplied as a container environment variable by the CI platform at runtime; none of the agent's declared capabilities (shell, fs.write) can modify the platform's own secret store.
A static secret value has no availability property that this agent's own actions could exhaust or deny.
The config file holds only tool, autonomy, and network settings; the secret value itself is injected via environment variable at runtime and is not stored as literal text in this file.
Editing a small YAML file has no availability impact distinct from the broader unbounded-execution risk already captured for the agent process in finding F4.
Artifacts do not describe transport-layer integrity controls (such as enforced TLS) for arbitrary outbound shell network connections.
Artifacts do not describe transport integrity controls for the push flow beyond assumed standard HTTPS to GitHub.
The Slack MCP server is only a stated future plan with no implementation details, so its authentication design cannot be assessed yet.
No tool definition or pinning details exist yet for the planned Slack integration to assess tampering risk against.
No logging design has been described for the planned Slack integration.
No rate-limiting or usage-cap design has been described for the planned Slack integration.
No credential-scoping design has been described yet for the planned Slack integration.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because untrusted GitHub issue content (openable and bug-labeled by any GitHub user) reaches irreversible, broadly-credentialed sinks (arbitrary shell execution, cross-repo push, and self-reconfiguration) under full autonomy with no step limits. The only present controls are two prompt-level instructions and a tool allowlist the agent can itself rewrite via cap.self_config, plus a container sandbox that leaves the network and credential sink unconstrained; together these earn at most one tier of credit (rubric step 4), leaving residual at high across all present-horizon findings. Two property findings (no step/runtime limit, no attributable audit trail) independently sit at high because the affected capabilities are consequential (execute, write, push, configure) under full autonomy. The forecast reaches critical because every credited control is behavioral or dependent on the model's own cooperation, including an allowlist the agent can edit via cap.self_config: a model upgrade, an autonomy increase, or the planned addition of a Slack MCP server each remove that one tier of credit, returning F1, F2, F3, and the Slack forecast finding to their inherent critical level and opening a new confidential-data egress channel. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctl.tool_allowlist, because the agent's own self_config capability lets it rewrite that allowlist without any external review.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP server configuration exists yet for the planned Slack integration; its capabilities, inputs, and trust model are inferred from a single sentence in the runtime notes and will need reassessment once implemented.
No CI/CD or branch protection rules were provided for the repositories the agent can push to; the cross-repo confused-deputy risk (F3) is assessed from the token scope alone.
No logging or monitoring configuration was provided; the absence of an audit trail (F5) is inferred from omission in the artifacts rather than a confirmed absence in the running system.
